title: Prevent Alzheimer’s dementia before irreversible functional loss

concept.text: The innovation would combine reliable identification of people at meaningful risk with an intervention that prevents Alzheimer’s dementia before substantial, irreversible loss of everyday function. It would need to interrupt disease early enough, remain effective long enough, and avoid harms that outweigh the benefit of treating people who may still feel healthy. The goal is a durable clinical benefit, rather than a change in a laboratory or imaging measurement alone.

Preventing clinical dementia is distinct from preventing the first detectable Alzheimer-related pathology. The June 2026 prevention-trial perspective uses primary prevention for intervention before detectable amyloid pathology. NRL-09 is defined by the eventual clinical outcome: preserving cognition and daily function before major loss. Preventing pathology could be one route to that outcome, but neither preventing amyloid accumulation nor clearing existing plaques would, by itself, demonstrate that dementia has been prevented.

significance.text: If safe, accessible prevention worked reliably for most at-risk people, a substantial cause of neurological disability would become preventable. The direct benefit would be more years with preserved cognition, independence and daily function. The supplied perspective motivates early intervention through the burden of Alzheimer disease and the possibility of interrupting its pathological cascade before symptoms develop; it does not establish that this outcome is already achievable.

Conditional impact synthesis: Broadly effective prevention could also reduce caregiving demands and long-term care needs. Those downstream benefits would depend on how many people benefit, how long protection lasts, treatment and monitoring burdens, affordability, and access. A result confined to a narrowly selected inherited-disease population would not establish comparable population-wide impact.

The impact has important boundaries. Preventing Alzheimer’s dementia would not automatically prevent dementia from other causes, and preserving function before injury would not establish an ability to rebuild damaged tissue or recover abilities already lost. A delay in symptom onset could be clinically valuable, but its significance would depend on its duration; delay during a finite study cannot establish lifelong prevention.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is the reliable combination of prediction and safe, durable clinical prevention. Presymptomatic risk identification already exists in some settings, particularly for people carrying mutations associated with dominantly inherited Alzheimer disease. The broader challenge is identifying people in the general population who are sufficiently likely to develop clinical disease, early enough for intervention to help. The perspective describes the substantial screening effort, cost and time required to recruit such populations.

A central biological uncertainty is whether the chosen intervention interrupts the processes that ultimately cause clinical deterioration. The perspective explicitly asks whether preventing or clearing larger amyloid plaques is sufficient to slow or stop long-term progression when an immunotherapy may not target amyloid seeds. Target engagement and plaque reduction therefore cannot be treated as interchangeable with preserved cognition or prevention of dementia.

Prevention also requires a workable treatment duration and safety profile for people without substantial impairment. Potentially prolonged or lifelong treatment raises questions about cumulative harms, sustained benefit and monitoring burden. Establishing the clinical outcome is itself difficult: the perspective explains that the long interval before clinical events makes maintaining a placebo comparison challenging and a clinical endpoint infeasible for its proposed platform, which instead uses biomarker outcomes.

current_state.text: The June 2026 perspective, “Primary prevention of Alzheimer disease in dominantly inherited Alzheimer network: a platform trial design,” documents active prevention research and describes planned or ongoing studies in inherited and sporadic Alzheimer disease. It is a trial-design perspective, not a completed demonstration of durable dementia prevention. The supplied review assessed its complete main-article HTML prose; figure images and supplementary documents were not inspected. Although the source index also lists a PDF, this record makes no claim of an additional assessment of that artifact.

That perspective reports preliminary evidence from an open-label gantenerumab extension involving asymptomatic people with dominantly inherited Alzheimer disease. Long-term treatment at doses associated with only partial amyloid-plaque removal may have substantially delayed first symptom onset. This is a reported preliminary finding in a rare inherited form of disease, rather than proof of durable prevention of clinical dementia in the general at-risk population. The underlying 2025 study report was not supplied, so its methods, effect estimates and uncertainties were not independently assessed in the review.

The earlier research describes lecanemab as producing less clinical decline and reduced amyloid markers, with adverse events, in an 18-month phase III trial of early symptomatic Alzheimer disease. Those details remain unverified within the supplied evidence: the retained PubMed copy contains only a cookie barrier, not the abstract or study text. The earlier assertion that the abstract was inspected therefore cannot be substantiated. This access limitation does not show that the reported findings are false, but the duration, trial phase, efficacy and harms cannot be presented here as verified results. Even as originally described, slowing decline after symptoms begin would not demonstrate presymptomatic prevention.

The DIAN-TU-002 platform described in the perspective uses biomarkers as its primary and key secondary outcomes because of the practical difficulty of waiting for clinical events. Such studies can test early biological effects and inform prevention strategies, but biomarker success alone would leave the central clinical question unresolved. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded search entries establishing whether subsequent results changed the picture by November 1, 2026; the dated June account should not be read as a verified account of all later developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: Large randomized trials beginning before substantial impairment should show a durable reduction in clinically meaningful Alzheimer’s dementia, accompanied by preserved daily function and acceptable long-term safety. The protocol should specify meaningful effect sizes, follow-up duration, dementia ascertainment and acceptable harm thresholds in advance. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established standards supplied by the reviewed paper.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trials demonstrate durable, safe dementia reduction preserving daily function

completion_criteria.text: Clinical outcomes would need to anchor the conclusion, with biomarker changes supporting interpretation of mechanism and treatment response. The perspective’s reliance on biomarker endpoints illustrates the feasibility problem: a practical early-stage platform can answer useful biological questions without completing the more demanding demonstration that dementia and functional loss have been prevented.
completion_criteria.label: Clinical outcomes demonstrate prevention of dementia and functional loss

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope requirements: Independent replication and sufficiently diverse study populations should establish who benefits, who does not, and how results differ between dominantly inherited and more common sporadic disease. Follow-up should distinguish sustained protection from a temporary postponement and examine whether benefit requires continued treatment. Finite trials would establish benefit across the populations and observation periods tested, rather than literal universality or lifelong protection.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes protection’s durability and scope across diverse populations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: Population-scale completion should also require a feasible route from risk identification to treatment and monitoring, with affordable access and an acceptable burden for people without symptoms. Strong efficacy in a specialized trial would establish a narrower achievement if screening costs, treatment harms or delivery requirements prevented broad use.
completion_criteria.label: Population-scale prevention is affordable and feasible for asymptomatic people

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: NRL-11, “Halt established Alzheimer’s disease and restore lost function,” is the closest companion. NRL-09 seeks to preserve function before substantial irreversible loss; NRL-11 addresses established disease and recovery afterward. Their biology and treatments could overlap, but success in either would not establish the other. The supplied roster confirms NRL-11’s title and this broad distinction; its detailed specification was not supplied.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain,” could enable a prevention strategy if that strategy required selective delivery. It is a general delivery capability, whereas NRL-09 requires evidence of clinical prevention. NRL-15, “Identify and treat shared mechanisms of neurodegeneration across diseases,” overlaps in disease-mechanism research, but a shared mechanism would need disease-specific validation before it could support an Alzheimer’s prevention claim.

Roster-based synthesis: NRL-04, “Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories,” and NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function,” concern repair or preservation of particular neural substrates. NRL-09 could succeed by preventing damage without acquiring either capability. Conversely, repairing a memory trace or replacing tissue would not by itself establish control of the continuing Alzheimer disease process. These remain distinct innovations.

change_log.change: Preserved NRL-09’s identity and expanded its explanation around integrated risk identification, early intervention and durable clinical benefit.
change_log.reason: The review supports a coherent unmet capability while clarifying that presymptomatic identification already exists in some settings.

change_log.change: Separated clinical dementia prevention from prevention of detectable amyloid pathology and from biomarker response.
change_log.reason: The perspective’s primary-prevention terminology concerns an earlier pathological stage, and plaque changes do not alone establish clinical prevention.

change_log.change: Specified the preliminary inherited-disease evidence as an open-label gantenerumab extension reported by the June 2026 perspective.
change_log.reason: This preserves the useful finding while making its design, population, indirect sourcing and limited generalizability explicit.

change_log.change: Corrected the claimed lecanemab abstract inspection and retained the earlier trial description only as explicitly unverified supplied research.
change_log.reason: The retained PubMed artifact is a cookie barrier. Preserving the qualified quantitative account avoids treating inaccessible evidence as either verified or disproven.

change_log.change: Added biological uncertainties about amyloid seeds and plaques, treatment duration, screening burden and the feasibility of clinical endpoints.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain why early biological activity has not yet established the proposed clinical capability.

change_log.change: Separated proposed completion requirements from the documented platform’s biomarker endpoints.
change_log.reason: Diversity, replication, clinical outcomes, safety and access are reasoned proposals for convincing completion, not established standards in the supplied source.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain related concepts, including NRL-11, without assuming their detailed specifications.
change_log.reason: The roster permits title-level comparison but does not establish the full scope of those entries.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access, inspection and freshness limitations in the relevant current-state paragraphs.
change_log.reason: The review assessed article prose, did not inspect figures or supplements, and did not establish completeness through the November as-of date.

unresolved_issues: The lecanemab paper’s identity and reported 18-month phase III efficacy and harms cannot be verified from the retained cookie-barrier artifact. The review’s recommendation to remove those details entirely was not adopted because the task requests preservation of unresolved quantitative detail with explicit qualification; they remain attributed to the earlier research rather than asserted as verified findings.
The underlying 2025 gantenerumab extension report was not supplied, leaving its methods, effect estimates and uncertainty unassessed beyond the perspective’s preliminary account.
It remains uncertain whether preventing or clearing amyloid plaques is sufficient to stop long-term clinical progression, and what treatment duration would provide durable protection.
Generalization from dominantly inherited disease to the broader sporadic at-risk population remains unestablished in the supplied evidence.
No supplied freshness search establishes whether later results changed the June 2026 account by November 1, 2026.
The proposed completion framework still requires concrete effect-size, follow-up, safety and practical-access thresholds; no numerical thresholds are established here.

brief.title: Preventing Alzheimer’s before independence is lost
possible: People at risk of Alzheimer’s could receive treatment while they still feel healthy and keep their memory, thinking and ability to manage daily life. This would require identifying who is likely to develop dementia early enough to prevent lasting loss.
why: Effective prevention would give people more years of independence. It could also reduce the demands on families and carers and the need for long-term care.

sources.who: Christopher H van Dyck and collaborators
sources.showed: Lecanemab slowed worsening of thinking and daily function over 18 months in people with early Alzheimer’s symptoms. It also reduced amyloid, a protein that forms deposits in the brain, but caused adverse effects.
sources.quote: Lecanemab reduced markers of amyloid in early Alzheimer's disease and resulted in moderately less decline on measures of cognition and function than placebo at 18 months but was associated with adverse events.
sources.cited_for: Treatment targeting amyloid can slow decline after symptoms begin.
sources.not_established: Slowing decline after symptoms begin does not establish prevention before symptoms or lasting protection.

sources.who: E. McDade and collaborators, DIAN-TU and DIAN-Obs
sources.showed: They describe a prevention trial platform for people with inherited Alzheimer’s risk. It measures biomarkers, biological signs of disease, to test treatment before detectable amyloid deposits develop.
sources.quote: This framework has enabled the launch of a platform trial incorporating biomarker outcomes that span successive phases of preclinical disease, allowing detection and quantification of downstream disease-modifying effects from preventing Aβ accumulation.
sources.cited_for: Trials can test early biological effects before symptoms appear.
sources.not_established: The trial design does not demonstrate that treatment prevents dementia or preserves daily function.

shown: Preliminary findings from the Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network suggest gantenerumab may delay first symptoms in people with a rare inherited form of Alzheimer’s. Participants knew they were receiving treatment. Durable prevention in the broader population remains unproven.
missing: Reliable early identification of people in the general population who are likely to develop Alzheimer’s dementia remains a challenge.
No treatment has demonstrated safe, durable prevention of Alzheimer’s dementia with preserved daily function.
A workable duration of preventive treatment, with acceptable long-term harms and monitoring demands, remains unknown.
An affordable route from screening to treatment and monitoring has yet to support prevention at population scale.

milestones.label: Trials show lasting prevention with acceptable safety
milestones.explanation: Large trials with randomly assigned treatment would have to reduce dementia durably, preserve daily function and meet agreed safety limits. This would establish benefit before substantial impairment.

milestones.label: People retain thinking and everyday abilities
milestones.explanation: Clinical outcomes would have to demonstrate prevention of dementia and functional loss, with biological measurements supporting the findings. This would establish that treatment protects people’s abilities.

milestones.label: Independent studies confirm who benefits and for how long
milestones.explanation: Independent studies in diverse populations would have to confirm protection and whether it requires continued treatment. This would distinguish lasting benefit from temporary delay and establish its scope.

milestones.label: Prevention becomes affordable and practical at population scale
milestones.explanation: Risk screening, treatment and monitoring would have to be affordable and manageable for people without symptoms. This would make prevention usable beyond specialized trials.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether preventing or clearing amyloid deposits is enough to stop long-term decline.
Protection in rare inherited Alzheimer’s may not translate to the more common form without those mutations.
The benefit, follow-up duration and acceptable harms needed to judge prevention successful still need concrete thresholds.

page.title: Pharmacological prevention of Alzheimer’s dementia
page.definition: A drug started before Alzheimer’s disease impairs a person’s cognition or daily function prevents or delays the onset of Alzheimer’s dementia. Dementia begins when cognitive decline interferes with everyday activities the person previously managed. Treatment may begin before Alzheimer’s pathology is detectable or while it is detectable but still causes no impairment. Clinical follow-up establishes who benefits and for how long.

goal.need: An estimated 7.4 million US adults aged 65 or older had clinical Alzheimer’s dementia in 2026. Families and other unpaid caregivers provided 19.6 billion hours of help in 2025 for Alzheimer’s and other dementias combined. Current antibody treatments start after cognitive impairment appears. Earlier treatment could act before extensive irreversible nerve-cell damage and give people more time to shop or pay bills independently. For people who still feel well, that benefit must outweigh the harms of treatment.

statements.body: FDA established an Alzheimer’s Prevention Accelerator within its neuroscience programme.
statements.quote: NAIN’s inaugural initiative, the Alzheimer's Prevention Accelerator, will focus on advancing medical products that help delay or prevent Alzheimer's disease.

statements.body: The Dominantly Inherited Alzheimer Network Trials Unit sets out a primary-prevention platform.
statements.quote: The goal of the DIAN-TU-002 study is to establish a platform protocol to accommodate multiple treatments
statements.context: The platform studies mutation carriers and uses biomarker outcomes as indicators of treatment effects.

statements.body: The Global CEO Initiative on Alzheimer’s Disease convened the expert group that defined target product profiles for preventive therapies.
statements.quote: Reduce rate of cognitive decline by at least 30%
statements.context: For biomarker-positive preclinical disease, the proposed minimum is 30% slower cognitive decline than with placebo over a period sufficient to show statistical significance. A better safety profile could justify a smaller effect. Preferred targets include at least 60% slower cognitive decline and a hazard ratio of 0.75 for progression to mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease or Alzheimer’s dementia.

completion.title: FDA grants traditional approval for a drug to prevent or delay Alzheimer’s dementia onset.
completion.criterion: FDA grants traditional marketing approval for a drug initiated before Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment, with an indication explicitly covering prevention or delay of Alzheimer’s dementia onset. The approved population, regimen and risk-management conditions define the scope of the achievement.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, traditional marketing approval for the specified indication and population.
completion.threshold_quote: benefits that outweigh its known and potential risks for the intended population
completion.basis: The preventive indication defines the clinical claim. FDA’s March 2024 draft guidance for early sporadic Alzheimer’s disease describes direct measures of clinical benefit and validated surrogate endpoints as possible grounds for traditional approval. Accelerated approval based on a surrogate reasonably likely to predict benefit is a different decision. Lecanemab’s traditional approval covered initiation at mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia.

milestones.title: A preventive drug has laboratory safety evidence sufficient to begin human testing.
milestones.criterion: Pharmacology and toxicology studies in animals or in vitro provide enough information for the sponsor to conclude that the proposed human investigation is reasonably safe. The nature and duration of the proposed investigation determine the scope of the nonclinical studies.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.23(a)(8), the preclinical safety requirement for an investigational new drug application.
milestones.threshold_quote: it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations.

milestones.title: A preventive candidate has human dose and safety data sufficient to design a phase 2 trial.
milestones.criterion: Human studies characterize the drug’s pharmacokinetics, pharmacological effects and adverse effects with increasing doses sufficiently to design a well-controlled phase 2 study. Phase 1 may enroll patients or healthy volunteers.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1), objectives of phase 1 investigations.
milestones.threshold_quote: to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: A preventive candidate engages its brain target before Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment.
milestones.criterion: An exploratory human study demonstrates that the drug engages its intended target in the brain in participants without Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment at baseline. A study enrolling several clinical stages must provide evidence for that baseline group.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Guideline on the clinical investigation of medicines for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease, section 4.4: exploratory-trial objectives.

milestones.title: A presymptomatic trial shows less cognitive decline under its prespecified efficacy test.
milestones.criterion: Show less cognitive decline than placebo on a prespecified efficacy test in participants without Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment at baseline. In PSEN1 E280A carriers, the Colombia trial specifies at least 260 weeks and tests annual rates of change on its cognitive composite and its memory cueing index at two-sided significance levels of 0.04 and 0.01, respectively. In sporadic preclinical disease, A45 tests superiority on change from baseline in the five-test Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite at 216 weeks.
milestones.set_by: Alzheimer’s Prevention Initiative Colombia trial protocol for PSEN1 E280A carriers and AHEAD A45 trial design for sporadic preclinical Alzheimer’s disease.
milestones.threshold_quote: superior to placebo on cognition, as measured by change from baseline of the PACC5 at 216 weeks

milestones.title: A placebo-controlled trial delays dementia after treatment starts before Alzheimer-related impairment.
milestones.criterion: A placebo-controlled trial starting before Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment demonstrates a clinically important delay in time to Alzheimer’s dementia. The prespecified event requires cognitive decline that interferes with activities the participant previously managed. EMA describes prevention follow-up as typically at least three years. An endpoint that combines mild cognitive impairment and dementia requires a separate analysis of dementia onset to establish this result.
milestones.set_by: European Medicines Agency, Guideline on the clinical investigation of medicines for the treatment of Alzheimer’s disease, sections 8.3.2 and 9: clinically important time-to-event outcomes and prevention trials.
milestones.threshold_quote:
an event of clear clinical importance (e.g.
time to dementia)

milestones.title: A preventive candidate demonstrates preclinical efficacy in an Alzheimer’s disease model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate that the candidate acts on its intended target in an established Alzheimer’s disease model or improves a disease-relevant outcome in that model. For a prevention experiment, begin treatment before the pathological or functional change under study and compare its subsequent development with a control group.
milestones.set_by: National Institute on Aging, Alzheimer’s Drug-Development Program, late-stage entry criteria for small molecules and biologics.
milestones.threshold_quote: The data package can include in vivo efficacy in an established AD animal model and/or in vivo target engagement.

not_found: No universal minimum dementia-onset delay or numerical ceiling on preventive-treatment harms was identified in the FDA and EMA guidance.
No positive randomized result meeting the dementia-onset milestone or corresponding FDA preventive indication was identified through 14 November 2026.

results.finding: In 1,169 cognitively unimpaired adults, solanezumab reduced amyloid-PET accumulation versus placebo by 7.7 centiloids.
results.detail: At 240 weeks, amyloid increased in both groups. The authors considered the slower accumulation consistent with target engagement, but noted limits on statistical inference. Solanezumab did not slow cognitive decline.
results.quote: Amyloid levels on brain PET increased by a mean of 11.6 centiloids in the solanezumab group and 19.3 centiloids in the placebo group.

results.finding: A4 solanezumab trial (1,169 randomized): 240-week cognitive score difference versus placebo was −0.30 points.
results.detail: The primary cognitive endpoint did not show a significant benefit: 95% CI −0.82 to 0.22; P = 0.26. Participants were cognitively unimpaired with elevated brain amyloid at enrollment.
results.quote: At 240 weeks, the mean change in PACC score was −1.43 in the solanezumab group and −1.13 in the placebo group (difference, −0.30; 95% confidence interval, −0.82 to 0.22; P = 0.26).

results.finding: In 1,169 cognitively unimpaired participants, solanezumab’s cognitive score change differed from placebo by −0.30.
results.detail: After 240 weeks, solanezumab did not significantly slow cognitive decline. Progression of the global CDR score included mild cognitive impairment, so it did not establish a delay in dementia onset.
results.quote: At 240 weeks, the mean change in PACC score was −1.43 in the solanezumab group and −1.13 in the placebo group (difference, −0.30; 95% confidence interval, −0.82 to 0.22; P = 0.26).

results.finding: Lecanemab lowered PET-measured brain amyloid by 59.1 centiloids versus placebo in 698 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease.
results.detail: The abstract describes enrollment by clinical stage and amyloid status. The Sporadic case assignment is inferred from that description.
results.quote: In a substudy involving 698 participants, there were greater reductions in brain amyloid burden with lecanemab than with placebo (difference, -59.1 centiloids; 95% CI, -62.6 to -55.6).

results.finding: Lecanemab reduced worsening on CDR-SB by 0.45 points versus placebo in 1,795 participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease.
results.detail: The Sporadic case assignment is inferred from the abstract’s description of enrollment by clinical stage and amyloid status.
results.quote: The adjusted least-squares mean change from baseline at 18 months was 1.21 with lecanemab and 1.66 with placebo (difference, -0.45; 95% confidence interval [CI], -0.67 to -0.23; P<0.001).

results.finding: In APPArcSwe mice (n=10/group), the lecanemab analog mAb158 reduced brain amyloid-beta protofibrils by 80% versus PBS.
results.detail: The integrated summary attributes the mouse effect to lecanemab, but the individual efficacy study descriptions identify mAb158 as the drug administered. In a separate experiment, all six Tg2576 mice dosed with lecanemab developed detectable anti-human antibodies.
results.quote:
Brain levels of Aβ protofibrils were decreased by 80% in mice 
dosed with mAb158, relative to controls.

results.finding: FDA issued lecanemab’s Study May Proceed Letter on October 27, 2010. The supplied text gives no sample size for the proposed first-in-human study.
results.detail: The review identifies the proposed treatment population as people with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer’s disease or mild Alzheimer’s dementia.
results.quote:
A Study May Proceed Letter was issued to the applicant on 
October 27, 2010.

results.finding: BAN2401 started human testing at 0.1 mg/kg after animal and toxicology studies. Nonclinical sample sizes were unreported.
results.detail: The paper gives no numerical NOAEL or safety margin and provides few details about the nonclinical studies. The safety conclusion applies to the proposed first-in-human study in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease.
results.quote:
No major issues in our animal studies, or in the formal
toxicological studies were seen. The starting dose was set
with an acceptable margin to NOAEL (No Observed
Adverse Effect Level).

results.finding: BAN2401 phase 1 (n=80) found a serum half-life of about 7 days, informing phase 2b dosing.
results.detail: The biomarkers gave no clear guidance on an effective dose, so phase 2b tested several doses and regimens. The criterion permits phase 1 enrollment of symptomatic patients.
results.quote:
The PK profile has guided us for
selecting dose and dose regimens in the ongoing
phase 2b study.

results.finding: BAN2401 phase 1 (n=80) found a 0.29% CSF-to-serum concentration ratio in the highest repeat-dose cohort.
results.detail: The highest repeat-dose cohort enrolled eight participants, six assigned BAN2401. The investigators lacked a validated assay for soluble Aβ protofibrils in human CSF.
results.quote:
In
this cohort, the CSF:serum ratio was 0.13 % at 24 h
after the final dose, and increased to 0.29 % at 14 days
after the final dose.

results.finding: In 53 initially asymptomatic mutation carriers assigned to gantenerumab or placebo, brain amyloid change differed by 33.3% between groups.
results.detail: The subgroup comparison was exploratory. The trial was not powered to detect differences in biomarker response between clinical stages.
results.quote: the relative change from baseline compared to shared placebo was larger in the asymptomatic group (33.3%: 15.9% reduction with gantenerumab versus 17.4% increase with placebo) compared to the symptomatic group

results.finding: Among 83 initially asymptomatic carriers, neither drug showed less cognitive decline than placebo. Estimated subgroup power was 5%.
results.detail: The analyzed baseline subgroup included 31 gantenerumab, 30 solanezumab and 22 placebo participants. The lack of measurable decline made treatment effects inconclusive, and practice effects may have contributed to improved memory scores.
results.quote: The asymptomatic groups showed no cognitive decline; symptomatic participants had declined before reaching the target doses.

results.finding: During gantenerumab dose escalation, 53% of 73 treated mutation carriers developed amyloid-related imaging abnormalities.
results.detail: Dose escalation occurred in an extension of a phase 2/3 trial.
results.quote: During the OLE period, the combined incidence of amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA), including both ARIA-E (cerebral edema/effusion) and ARIA-H (hemorrhage), was 53% (39/73).

results.finding: Gantenerumab reduced brain amyloid by 0.71 PiB-PET SUVR at year 3 in the 55-participant mixed-stage analysis.
results.detail: The primary PET model compared change from extension baseline within the treated cohort.
results.quote: At the final analysis, the adjusted mean change from OLE baseline to year 3 in PiB-PET SUVR was −0.71 SUVR (95% CI −0.88 to −0.53, p<0.0001).

results.finding: Gantenerumab showed no significant cognitive composite benefit in asymptomatic carriers (43 treated, 73 controls, p=0.64).
results.detail: The DIAN-TU extension used its own cognitive composite.
results.quote: The Functional Assessment Scale, MMSE, and OLE cognitive composite outcomes showed no significant differences in the annual rate of change between the gantenerumab treated group (OLE period data only) and the main set of controls for either the OLE baseline asymptomatic group or baseline symptomatic group

results.finding: For the longest-treated gantenerumab group, recurrent CDR-SB progression had an HR of 0.53 (22 treated, 86 extended controls).
results.detail: The recurrent CDR-SB confidence interval included 1 against the main control set. The paper gives no separate time-to-dementia analysis.
results.quote: When comparing the treatment group with the extended control group (n = 86), the hazard ratio (95% CI) is 0.40 (0.14 to 1.16) for time to first progression in CDR global and 0.53 (0.29 to 0.97) for time to recurrent progression in CDR-SB

results.finding: Crenezumab lowered soluble brain amyloid-β in hAPP transgenic mice after two weekly 5 mg/kg doses. Sample size unreported.
results.detail: The protocol does not quantify the amyloid-β reduction.
results.quote:
Furthermore, administration of 2 weekly doses of 5 mg/kg crenezumab to hAPP Tg 
mice decreased total A levels in soluble fractions of brain homogenates while 
increasing plasma total A levels.

results.finding: Cynomolgus monkeys tolerated weekly subcutaneous crenezumab up to 100 mg/kg. Sample size unreported.
results.detail: Microscopic injection-site infiltrates reversed during the 14-week dose-free period.
results.quote:
Weekly SC administrations of crenezumab to cynomolgus monkeys for 39 weeks 
(total of 40 doses) was well-tolerated at doses of up to 100 mg/kg (highest dose tested).

results.finding: Cynomolgus monkeys tolerated weekly subcutaneous crenezumab up to 100 mg/kg. Sample size unreported.
results.detail: The sponsor used the same nonclinical package to support the sporadic program and the autosomal-dominant Phase II trial.
results.quote:
Overall, results from nonclinical safety and pharmacology studies supported the clinical 
development program of crenezumab in sporadic AD, as well as this Phase II study in 
ADAD.

results.finding: Human dose and safety data supported adding 60 mg/kg IV crenezumab to autosomal-dominant Phase II. Supporting sample size unreported for the dose decision.
results.detail: The Phase Ib study used symptomatic patients. The criterion permits phase 1 studies in patients or healthy volunteers.
results.quote:
Specifically, the dose of 60 mg/kg 
IV every 4 weeks (Q4W) was included as an option for participants in this study 
(GN28352, amendment 6).

results.finding: In mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease, crenezumab exposure rose proportionally through 120 mg/kg IV in Phase Ib. Sample size for the PK analysis unreported.
results.detail: The protocol reports a denominator of 75 for the Phase Ib immunogenicity analysis. It does not give a denominator for its pharmacokinetic analysis.
results.quote:
In the Phase Ib Study GN29632 investigating treatment doses of up to 120 mg/kg, there 
was no relationship between the treatment dose and the incidence or type of injection 
and infusion-related adverse events.

results.finding: In two atabecestat phase 1 trials (n=63), 50% of European participants at 50 mg reported a treatment-emergent adverse event.
results.detail: The 50-mg adverse-event rate was based on 16 European participants. The study also assessed CNS exposure and biomarker response to inform dose selection.
results.quote:
3 of 15 patients (20.0%) in
the atabecestat 10-mg group, in 8 of 16 patients in 50-mg
group (50.0%), and in 4 of 14 patients (28.6%) in the pla-
cebo group.

results.finding: In Japanese participants with preclinical Alzheimer’s disease (n=18), atabecestat 50 mg reduced mean CSF Aβ1–40 by 87.15% from baseline.
results.detail: The 87.15% reduction was measured after four weeks in the six participants assigned to 50 mg. The Japanese cohort provides evidence specific to the unimpaired baseline group.
results.quote:
Mean percent reduc-
tions for 10 mg and 50 mg vs. placebo were 67.3 –89.9%
vs. 3.3% in Caucasian early AD and 68.21 –87.15% vs.
7.36% in Japanese preclinical AD, respectively.

results.finding: In European participants with early Alzheimer’s disease (n=45), atabecestat showed no significant placebo difference on computerized cognitive tests at day 28.
results.detail: The trial assessed cognition to detect unexpected adverse effects over four weeks. Its cohort-level results combine preclinical disease and mild cognitive impairment.
results.quote:
The
LS mean difference of each of the atabecestat groups
compared with placebo was not significant.

results.finding: CAD106 slowed brain amyloid accumulation in cognitively unimpaired APOE ε4 homozygotes (PET n=51, P<0.001).
results.detail: Participants entered with or without elevated brain amyloid. The exploratory subgroup without elevated baseline amyloid was small (n=14, unadjusted P=0.071).
results.quote: slower rates of Aβ plaque accumulation (mean [standard deviation] annualized change from baseline in amyloid PET Centiloid: −0.91[5.65] for CAD106 versus 8.36 [6.68] for placebo;  P  < 0.001)

results.finding: The CAD106 trial (n=65 randomized) found no exploratory cognitive benefit. Mean RBANS change was 1.4 points lower with CAD106.
results.detail: The last cognitive assessment was at 18–24 months. The paper does not give the number assessed for RBANS at that visit.
results.quote: There was no difference between CAD106 and placebo in the mean change from baseline in the RBANS total score up to the last assessment, as shown by the small mean changes and the large SD (−1.0 [9.27] for CAD106 and +0.4 [7.20] for placebo at the last assessment [Year 2 visit]).

results.finding: Crenezumab dose escalation in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer’s disease (n=75 dosed) found zero protocol-defined dose-limiting toxicities.
results.detail: The placebo-controlled period lasted 13 weeks. Further follow-up was open-label, and participants assigned the highest dose switched to 60 mg/kg.
results.quote: Overall, most AEs were low grade and no protocol-defined dose-limiting toxicities or deaths occurred.

results.finding: Exploratory amyloid PET in the crenezumab extension (n=71 enrolled) suggested stable cortical amyloid uptake at doses of 45 mg/kg or higher.
results.detail: The study lacked power to detect imaging differences. The extension enrollment count is 71, and the text does not specify how many participants contributed follow-up PET scans.
results.quote: Amyloid PET SUVR using the subcortical white matter as a reference region suggested that participants who received the higher doses (45 and 60 mg/kg IV q4w) may have stabilized SUVR over time, whereas mean SUVR in participants in the lowest dose group (30 mg/kg IV q4w) increased

results.finding: In A4 (1,169 randomized), brain amyloid PET burden increased by 7.7 centiloids less with solanezumab than with placebo.
results.detail: The imaging analysis provided multiplicity-unadjusted confidence intervals that the authors said could not be used for statistical inference.
results.quote: Amyloid levels on brain PET increased by a mean of 11.6 centiloids in the solanezumab group and 19.3 centiloids in the placebo group.

results.finding: In A4 (1,169 randomized), the PACC change with solanezumab was 0.30 points worse than with placebo.
results.detail: The primary analysis included 1,147 participants in the modified intention-to-treat population.
results.quote: At 240 weeks, the mean change in PACC score was −1.43 in the solanezumab group and −1.13 in the placebo group (difference, −0.30; 95% confidence interval, −0.82 to 0.22; P = 0.26).

results.finding: In A4 (1,169 randomized), estimated progression to mild cognitive impairment or dementia was 3 percentage points higher with solanezumab than with placebo.
results.detail: The arm-specific estimates in Table 2 use a Kaplan–Meier analysis. Progression required two consecutive nonzero global CDR scores or a nonzero score at the final visit.

results.finding: In 168 treated PSEN1 Glu280Ala carriers, crenezumab showed no significant amyloid plaque removal over 5–8 years.
results.detail: The prespecified imaging measure was annualised change in florbetapir PET uptake, which measures fibrillar plaque burden.
results.quote: secondary and exploratory outcomes also showed no significant effect on removal of amyloid plaques or other clinical or biomarker outcomes.

results.finding: In 168 treated PSEN1 Glu280Ala carriers, crenezumab did not significantly slow decline on the API ADAD composite (p=0.43).
results.quote: The annualised rate of change in the API ADAD composite was −1·10 (SE 0·29) in the crenezumab group and −1·43 (0·29) in the placebo group (between-group difference 0·33 [95% CI −0·48 to 1·13]; p=0·43).

results.finding: The crenezumab trial in 168 treated PSEN1 Glu280Ala carriers showed no significant secondary clinical benefit over 5–8 years.
results.quote: secondary and exploratory outcomes also showed no significant effect on removal of amyloid plaques or other clinical or biomarker outcomes.

results.finding: In PSAPP mice (n = 5 per group), prophylactic 776890 reduced cortical and hippocampal amyloid deposition by more than twofold versus vehicle.
results.quote: Image analysis in the cortex and hippocampus of 6-mo-old PSAPP mice (prophylactic group) showed a highly significant (greater than twofold; P < 0.01) attenuation of cerebral amyloidosis by chronic treatment with compound 2 ( Fig. 7, A and B ).

results.finding: Bumetanide improved spatial learning versus vehicle in aged female APOE4 knock-in mice (11 per group, P = 0.0345).
results.detail: Dosing began six weeks before water maze testing. The study did not establish whether the learning deficit was already present when dosing began.
results.quote:
In sum, these data demonstrate 
that bumetanide treatment restored normal spatial learning in aged 
APOE4-KI mice.

results.finding: In Ts65Dn mice (n = 4 per group), DS-01 preserved medial septal cholinergic neuron size, with cell bodies ~10% larger than in vehicle controls.
results.detail: The authors based the pretreatment timing on prior evidence that cholinergic neuron size is normal at 5 months and atrophy emerges after 6 months.
results.quote: The area of ChAT-positive (ChAT+) cell bodies was significantly larger by ~10% in DS-01 versus-vehicle-treated Ts65Dn mice

results.finding: In TOP-COG (21 adults with Down syndrome randomized), the Memory for Objects confidence interval suggested a standardized benefit of at least 0.4 with simvastatin.
results.detail: Recruitment and retention were the primary outcomes. Memory for Objects was one of eight secondary cognitive measures and was proposed as the primary outcome for a future definitive trial.
results.quote: The CI for the effect size estimates with this outcome suggests the true effect size from simvastatin treatment to be at least 0.4.

results.finding: In a vitamin E trial in adults with Down syndrome (337 randomized, 249 dementia-free at baseline), incident dementia was 8 percentage points higher with vitamin E than with placebo.
results.detail: The 8-percentage-point difference is calculated from the reported rounded percentages.
results.quote: The vitamin E group had 44 cases of incident dementia (37%) and the placebo group had 36 (29%)

definition = "A drug started before Alzheimer\u2019s disease impairs a person\u2019s cognition or daily function prevents or delays the onset of Alzheimer\u2019s dementia. Dementia begins when cognitive decline interferes with everyday activities the person previously managed. Treatment may begin before Alzheimer\u2019s pathology is detectable or while it is detectable but still causes no impairment. Clinical follow-up establishes who benefits and for how long.". Reason: Defining impairment as a decline from the person’s own baseline makes the definition applicable to people with lifelong disabilities and clarifies when treatment can begin.

goal.need = "An estimated 7.4 million US adults aged 65 or older had clinical Alzheimer\u2019s dementia in 2026. Families and other unpaid caregivers provided 19.6 billion hours of help in 2025 for Alzheimer\u2019s and other dementias combined. Current antibody treatments start after cognitive impairment appears. Earlier treatment could act before extensive irreversible nerve-cell damage and give people more time to shop or pay bills independently. For people who still feel well, that benefit must outweigh the harms of treatment.". Reason: The 2026 estimates quantify the burden, and the revised paragraph explains what delaying dementia would mean for patients and families.

add statement by The Global CEO Initiative on Alzheimer’s Disease convened the expert group that defined target product profiles for preventive therapies., 2026: "Reduce rate of cognitive decline by at least 30%". Reason: The profiles distinguish a target for cognitive decline from a target for progression to mild cognitive impairment or dementia.

edit completion: criterion = "FDA grants traditional marketing approval for a drug initiated before Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment, with an indication explicitly covering prevention or delay of Alzheimer\u2019s dementia onset. The approved population, regimen and risk-management conditions define the scope of the achievement."; set_by = "US Food and Drug Administration, traditional marketing approval for the specified indication and population."; set_by_kind = "regulator"; threshold_quote = "benefits that outweigh its known and potential risks for the intended population"; threshold_ref = 6; basis = "The preventive indication defines the clinical claim. FDA\u2019s March 2024 draft guidance for early sporadic Alzheimer\u2019s disease describes direct measures of clinical benefit and validated surrogate endpoints as possible grounds for traditional approval. Accelerated approval based on a surrogate reasonably likely to predict benefit is a different decision. Lecanemab\u2019s traditional approval covered initiation at mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia."; refs = [6, 7, 8]. Reason: The revised basis distinguishes the preventive indication from FDA’s general evidentiary standard and gives the early-disease draft guidance its correct scope.
add case "Down syndrome–associated". Reason: A randomized prevention study in adults with Down syndrome establishes a distinct disease form with its own clinical evidence.

add milestone after None: "A preventive candidate demonstrates preclinical efficacy in an Alzheimer’s disease model.". Reason: The existing sequence starts with safety for human testing and omits the earlier demonstration that a candidate acts on Alzheimer’s pathology in a laboratory model.

edit m1: criterion = "Pharmacology and toxicology studies in animals or in vitro provide enough information for the sponsor to conclude that the proposed human investigation is reasonably safe. The nature and duration of the proposed investigation determine the scope of the nonclinical studies."; threshold_quote = "it is reasonably safe to conduct the proposed clinical investigations."; threshold_ref = 10; refs = [10]. Reason: The criterion should state the safety judgment needed for the proposed human exposure without embedding a lecanemab review for symptomatic disease.

edit m2: criterion = "Human studies characterize the drug\u2019s pharmacokinetics, pharmacological effects and adverse effects with increasing doses sufficiently to design a well-controlled phase 2 study. Phase 1 may enroll patients or healthy volunteers."; set_by = "FDA, 21 CFR 312.21(a)(1), objectives of phase 1 investigations."; threshold_quote = "to permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies."; threshold_ref = 12; refs = [12]. Reason: The phase 1 criterion applies across disease forms and does not require the doses or exposure duration used in a particular symptomatic trial.

edit m3: title = "A preventive candidate engages its brain target before Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment."; criterion = "An exploratory human study demonstrates that the drug engages its intended target in the brain in participants without Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment at baseline. A study enrolling several clinical stages must provide evidence for that baseline group."; threshold_quote = "Demonstration of target engagement"; threshold_ref = 14; refs = [14]. Reason: The revised criterion specifies whose target engagement must be demonstrated and removes trial outcomes from the test.

edit m4: criterion = "Show less cognitive decline than placebo on a prespecified efficacy test in participants without Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment at baseline. In PSEN1 E280A carriers, the Colombia trial specifies at least 260 weeks and tests annual rates of change on its cognitive composite and its memory cueing index at two-sided significance levels of 0.04 and 0.01, respectively. In sporadic preclinical disease, A45 tests superiority on change from baseline in the five-test Preclinical Alzheimer Cognitive Composite at 216 weeks."; set_by = "Alzheimer\u2019s Prevention Initiative Colombia trial protocol for PSEN1 E280A carriers and AHEAD A45 trial design for sporadic preclinical Alzheimer\u2019s disease."; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "superior to placebo on cognition, as measured by change from baseline of the PACC5 at 216 weeks"; threshold_ref = 17; refs = [19, 17]. Reason: The Colombia protocol supplies a cognitive efficacy test specifically for presymptomatic mutation carriers, correcting the reliance on a mixed-stage analysis.

edit m5: title = "A placebo-controlled trial delays dementia after treatment starts before Alzheimer-related impairment."; criterion = "A placebo-controlled trial starting before Alzheimer-related cognitive impairment demonstrates a clinically important delay in time to Alzheimer\u2019s dementia. The prespecified event requires cognitive decline that interferes with activities the participant previously managed. EMA describes prevention follow-up as typically at least three years. An endpoint that combines mild cognitive impairment and dementia requires a separate analysis of dementia onset to establish this result."; threshold_quote = "an event of clear clinical importance (e.g.\ntime to dementia)"; threshold_ref = 14; refs = [14, 23]. Reason: The revised test identifies dementia onset as the event and keeps findings about earlier impairment in an open-label extension out of the criterion.
